catalog_quote: From 1995 to 2004, I have done fieldwork on: Dììr, Bili (Buli), Nyámzax (Langas), Posə (Polci) and Luri. ... As a convention, I will call the Polci cluster ‘Polci’ and the Polci language ‘Po’. Po and Za are three-tone languages (Lo = à; Mid = a; Hi = á); the others are two-tone languages (Lo = à; Hi = a). This will make it difficult for the time being to mark tones on CP

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: has a text; extracted text of p.2 (= p.1 of the paper, introduction, immediately before 'Abbreviations' and '1. Pronouns') reads exactly: "As a convention, I will call the Polci cluster 'Polci' and the Polci language 'Po'. Po and Za are three-tone languages (Lo = à; Mid = a; Hi = á); the others are two-tone languages (Lo = à; Hi = a). This will make it difficult for the time being to mark tones on CP" -- verbatim as reported (curly vs straight quotes only). I re-read the whole 7-page paper: it is comparative pronominal/TAM morphology of Common Polci vs Zaar; the only prosodic content is this tone-level sentence plus tonal 2s/2p contrasts ('Po marks 2p with a Lo tone on the TAM'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pesse (Caron's 'Po', the Polci language proper) is described as a three-level tone language (Low, Mid, High), like Zaar and unlike the other Polci-cluster languages, which have two tones. No opened source says anything about word stress or accent in Pesse; no stress rule can be stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Caron notes only that the 3-tone vs 2-tone difference makes tone-marking of reconstructed Common Polci forms difficult.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the lexical/grammatical tone system; it comes from a 7-page conference paper on comparative morphology, not from a phonological description, so silence on stress is not evidence of absence.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog polc1243 'Pesse' is the Polci language proper (autonym Pesse [pəsə]; Polci/Polchi/Palci, Posɨ in Shimizu 1978, Pəlci in Kraft 1981, Posə/'Po' in Caron 2005), ISO 639-3 pze, created in 2023 when plj 'Polci' was split into Pesse [pze], Ɓuli [uly], Zul [zlu] and Nyamzak-Dir-Mbarimi [nzr] (ISO CR 2022-023). Caron's quoted statement is explicitly about 'Po' = the Polci language (this variety), as distinct from the 'Polci cluster' (Zul, Baram, Dir, Buli, Langas/Nyamzax, Lundur, Luri), whose other members he describes as two-tone. Spoken in c. 45 settlements, Polchi District (Dass LGA) and Toro LGA, Bauchi State; c. 37,000 speakers (Aregbesola 2022).

new_statements.quote: Le polci a également un système à trois tons que l'on peut supposer influencé par les contacts avec le zarek, qui a également été décrit avec trois tons par Lukas et Willms. [sec. 6.1 Phonologie, PDF p. 9] — and, introduction, PDF pp. 2-3: D'un point de vue phonologique, la majorité des langues SBW ont deux tons, alors que le zaar et le gùùs en ont trois.
new_statements.translation: Polci also has a three-tone system, which one may suppose to have been influenced by contact with Zarek, which was likewise described with three tones by Lukas and Willms. — From a phonological point of view, most SBW languages have two tones, whereas Zaar and Gùùs have three.
new_statements.citation: Caron, Bernard. 2009. Les Zaars et leurs voisins. 16 pp. HAL halshs-00643986. p.7, sec. 6.1 Phonologie: 'Le polci a egalement un systeme a trois tons.' (corroborates Caron 2005; nothing on stress).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: extracted text per page: p.9 (printed page number 8 at foot) lines 1-5: 'On a déjà signalé le développement de systèmes tonals à 3 niveaux en zaar. On retrouve ce phénomène au sud de la zone en angas, mwaghavul et dans les langues ron. Le polci a également un système à trois tons que l'on peut supposer influencé par les contacts avec le zarek, qui a également été décrit avec trois tons par Lukas et Willms.' -- verbatim match; the heading '6.1 Phonologie' sits at the foot of p.8 (printed 7), as the compiler said. p.2 last line into p.3 first line: 'D'un point de vue phonologique, la majorité des langues SBW ont deux tons, alors que le zaar et le gùùs2 en ont trois.' -- verbatim (the '2' is a…
new_statements.relation_note: Read in full (all 16 PDF pages). The paper is an areal-contact study of the SBW languages; its phonology paragraphs (sec. 4.2, 5.2, 6.1) discuss vowel inventories, consonant series and tone levels only. The words 'accent', 'tonique', 'prosodie', 'stress' do not occur anywhere. It states that Polci has a three-tone system (against two tones in most SBW languages), which agrees with the existing statement from Caron 2005 ('Po and Za are three-tone languages'). Nothing on word stress. The general remark in sec. 5.2 that the region's Chadic languages have 4 tones (2 level + 2 contour) 'à l'exception du zaar' concerns the SBW group as a whole, not Polci specifically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Polci is described as a three-level tone language (Lo, Mid, Hi), unusual within South Bauchi West where two tones are the norm; no word-stress rule is stated and stress is not mentioned at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Caron 2009 lists the Polci cluster as zùl, baram, dir, buli, langas (=nyamzax), lundur and 'polci (=posə)'; the three-tone statement concerns the Polci language proper (Posə = Pesse, ISO pze after the 2023 split of plj), i.e. polc1243, not the cluster as a whole. Decker & Aregbesola 2022 treats the same six varieties as separate languages and calls polc1243 'Pesse (Polci)'.
